title: Three friendships
hookLine: Aristotle: friendships of use, of pleasure, and of goodness (Nicomachean Ethics 8.3)

cards: A crowded group chat. Some people are in it because you work together, some because you have fun together. And maybe one or two are there because, if everything else fell away, you'd still want them in your life.
Aristotle noticed the same sorting long before phones, in his Nicomachean Ethics, and he gave it a shape: three kinds of friendship, and a slow one at the end.

teach.b: First, friends of use. Some friendships rest on what each person gets: a coworker, a neighbor who lends tools. Aristotle doesn't sneer at these, but when the usefulness ends, he says, the friendship tends to end too.
Second, friends of pleasure: people who are fun, who make you laugh. He notices these among the young, who change what they enjoy, and so make and lose friends quickly.
Third, friends of the good. The complete kind, Aristotle says, is between people who are good and alike in goodness, who wish good to each other for the other's own sake.
These turn out pleasant and useful too, but that isn't why they exist, and they last as long as the people stay good.
Fourth, salt eaten together. Such friendships are rare, he says, and slow. As the old saying goes, people can't know each other until they've eaten salt together.
The wish for friendship comes fast; the friendship itself takes time.
Philia is Aristotle's word for all three kinds. He doesn't call friends of use fake. He calls them a smaller kind, and keeps the larger kind for people who want each other's good.

how: Aristotle's three kinds of friendship, from books eight and nine of the Nicomachean Ethics, are studied in philosophy and ethics courses, and some readers use them to reflect on their own friendships.

games.q: you're Aristotle. a friendship of pleasure stops being fun. what does your book say tends to happen?
o: it turns into a friendship of the good.
games.why: when the pleasure or the use ends, he says, the friendship tends to end too. the friendship of the good lasts as long as the people stay good.

practice: Let a few friends' faces come to mind, without ranking them, and notice gently which friendships rest on use, which on enjoyment, and whether one rests on wanting each other's good.

If one name stands out, stay with it and remember the time it took, the meals and the hard days, the salt eaten together. If no name comes, that's an honest answer too, and a friendship like that can still begin.

wordCard.voice: Philia. The Greek word for the love between friends. Aristotle used it for all three kinds: friends of use, of pleasure, and of the good. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the love between friends; Aristotle's word for all three kinds of friendship.
